Chapter 9 273
Summary
This chapter packed a punch by covering various new concepts surrounding MCP. We used what
we have already learned to apply these concepts in the context of network monitoring and per-
formance. Then, we took the same code and applied it to an MCP version. We learned about
various foundational concepts, such as URIs and resources versus tools, before discovering more
advanced concepts, such as tool chaining, workflow orchestration, and production consideration.
MCP aims to standardize AI capability exposure instead of needing to build custom APIs for each
tool. It provides a unified interface and the ability to chain together multiple tools to create a
comprehensive platform. The AI-assisted field is moving so fast that there might be another new
feature coming out by the time you read this book; however, the road toward standardization,
integration, and solving real-world problems faster and better will be consistent, regardless of
any new tools.
In the next chapter, we will investigate using AI-assisted coding, also known as vibe coding, for
network security use cases.
Get This Book’s PDF Version and
Exclusive Extras
Scan the QR code (or go to packtpub.com/unlock). Search for this
book by name, confirm the edition, and then follow the steps on
the page.
Note: Keep your invoice handy. Purchases made directly from Packt
don’t require an invoice.
10
Network Security through Vibe
Coding
One of the areas where AI-assisted tasks shine the most is writing code. Compared to human
languages, computer languages are much easier for computers to master. Computer program-
ming languages, such as Python, are designed to be unambiguous and highly structured. Each
statement, parameter, or keyword follows a clearly defined grammar and syntax rules. If we miss a
closing bracket or a comma, the program will simply fail to run until we correct the syntax mistake.
On the other hand, human languages are ambiguous and rely heavily on cultural and contextual
references. Take the following sentence as an example: “Eric writes code in Python; it is his fa-
vorite coding language.” To English speakers, the “it” in the second part of the sentence naturally
refers to the language ‘Python,’ but it is a (surprisingly) difficult task for computers to know that
contextual reference with accuracy.
This is why coding assistance was one of the first areas where AI LLMs really shone. Often re -
ferred to as vibe coding in the community, it generally refers to the translation layer of converting
humans’ ambiguous and unstructured natural language tasks into computer code. When we
are brainstorming or prototyping, we can describe our thoughts to this vibe code tool, and it will
translate the intent into code.
Network Security through Vibe Coding 276
In this chapter, we will introduce vibe coding in the context of network security. While vibe coding

chunks.title: ainetworkingcookbook
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 273
chunks.content:
can be applied whenever we need to write code, network security is a great fit for vibe coding for
the following reasons:
• Security operations often require rapid prototyping and iterative development of detec-
tion scripts
• Security experts are often not top-tier coders; they need the code to be good enough, but
also to match the security expert’s intent
• Vibe coding is conversational and exploratory, which can quickly turn conversation into
code instead of formal software development cycles
• We can develop custom security tools that are more fitted to us than generic solutions
that we can purchase
• Vibe coding’s iterative nature matches how security professionals often need to quickly
adapt and modify their security logic
In this chapter, we will cover the following recipes:
• Setting up GitHub Copilot
• Setting up Claude Code
• Conversational log analysis and threat detection
• Rapid security script development for incident response
Please keep in mind that vibe coding, by definition, will yield different results every single time.
For the recipes in this chapter, focus on the flow, prompt, and process; your result will 100% be
different than what you see on these pages.
Technical requirements
As with the other chapters in this book, please create a folder for the recipes for this chapter, as
well as a Python virtual environment:
$ mkdir ch10 && cd ch10
$ pyhon -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

At the time of writing, there are generally two ways to “vibe code.” The first is to integrate the
tool inside your Integrated Development Environment (IDE); the other, newer approach is to
integrate the tool in the terminal. Using the IDE is more familiar to folks who already use IDEs
to write code, while the terminal is more universal (for example, it can be found on your mobile
phone). We will illustrate both approaches, using GitHub Copilot with Visual Studio (VS) Code
for the first approach and Anthropic Claude Code for the second approach.
This field is quickly evolving, so please check out the following resources for the latest pricing and
installation options if you find them to be different compared to what’s mentioned in this chapter:
• GitHub Copilot: https://github.com/features/copilot
• Anthropic Claude Code: https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code

Having the ability to vibe code within an IDE is great. However, not every platform is suited to be

10.4 Rapid security script development for incident
response
In this recipe, we will use Claude Code to rapidly develop incident response automation. Just like
in the Conversational log analysis and threat detection recipe, we will use a conversational style to
complete this task.
Getting ready
Please complete the Setting up Claude Code recipe and copy the mock data files, incident_
scenarios.json and network_topology.yaml, from this book’s GitHub repository (https://
github.com/PacktPublishing/AI-Networking-Cookbook-First-Edition).
How to do it…
1. Start Claude Code by typing claude in the terminal prompt.
Network Security through Vibe Coding 298
2. Since this is just a terminal, we can use all of the Linux tools available in the prompt, such
as pwd, cd, and ls.
Figure 10.19: Claude with Linux tools
3. Start a conversation by typing I need to build an incident response system that
can automatically isolate infected systems, block malicious IPs, and collect
forensic evidence. The system should handle different incident types, such
as ransomware, data exfiltration, and credential compromise. Please help
me design this from the ground up.
4. Claude Code will list out a few steps and start its work on the process.
Figure 10.20: Claude Code’s design solution

create the file or iterate on the script.
Figure 10.21: Claude Code creating an incident_response_system.py file
6. Start to engage in other conversations, such as What is the best way to structure this
so that it can handle multiple incident types and integrate with different
security tools?.
How it works…
The Claude Code conversation approach to incident response development provides several
advantages over simple code completion:
• Natural language problem-solving: Claude Code maintains context across complex,
multi-turn discussions.
• Architectural guidance: Claude arguably has a better understanding of architectural
guidance. Whether it is better than, say, GitHub Copilot is a judgment call, but it is defi -
nitely better than traditional code completion.
• Terminal integration: Claude Code directly integrates into the terminal and offers a
smoother experience for experienced CLI users.
Network Security through Vibe Coding 300
• Iterative refinement: Just like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code allows for real-time refine -
ment of response logic, escalation procedures, and integration approaches based on user
feedback.
There’s more…
Claude Code can also work with Python code if we use claude-code-sdk on PyPI: https://docs.
anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/sdk#python. The following terminal command installs
claude-code-sdk for Python:
$ pip install claude-code-sdk

chunks.heading: Chapter 10 301
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 301
Summary
In this chapter, we introduced vibe coding as a conversational approach to developing network
security automation. Unlike the traditional development approach, vibe coding prioritizes rapid
prototyping through natural language conversation with AI assistants. Some of its core concepts
include the following:
• Conversation over formal specification requirements: Instead of providing a formal
document, security professionals just describe the problem and intended solutions
• Speed over perfection: We rarely get the script right the first time, or the second time,
but since the time-to-script is so fast, we get to iterate really quickly
• Domain expertise first: Vibe coding allows subject matter experts to leverage their domain
expertise, and allows the vibe coding tool to write code
Using GitHub Copilot, we are able to use vibe coding directly in VS Code. The assistant can behave
in Ask or Agent mode, with a different mix-and-match of models to choose from. With Claude
Code, the vibe coding assistant is integrated into the terminal.
This is the last chapter of this book. Thank you for taking this journey with me through the evolving
landscape at the intersection of AI LLMs and network engineering. The time and effort you have
invested in this book should serve you well for the fundamental shift in how network professionals
can solve complex problems. This book is intended as your starting point, not the destination.
The real magic happens when you take these patterns and adapt them for your own usage.
I want to thank you again for giving this book a piece of your time. I hope the solutions provided
have offered value to you, and I want to wish you the best of luck on your AI LLM network engi-
neering journey. The future of network engineering will be written by practitioners like you, using
AI to amplify and not to replace human engineers. Onward and upward!
